newsitem.title: FRANCE: European currency parities correct - Lamfalussy.
newsitem.headline: European currency parities correct - Lamfalussy.

text.p: The head of the European Union's future central bank said on Thursday that the parities between Europe's major currencies, including the franc and the mark, were now correct.

"The parities overall, not only between the franc and the mark, seem to me correct," Alexandre Lamfalussy, head of the European Monetary Institute, said in an interview published in afternoon daily Le Monde.

"As for the franc, whatever indices we look at, its bilateral exchange rate compared to the mark, or the effective real rate compared to the group of currencies, we see for years a great stability. We can even see a certain improvement in the competitiveness of the country. I really do not see a problem."
Lamfalussy's was speaking on the eve of the EU Dublin summit called to push forward reform of EU institutions and pave the way for the start of a single European currency in 1999.
EU finance ministers were meeting in advance on Thursday to address a "stability pact" for countries in the euro zone.
The pact, proposed by Germany to ensure budgetary discipline for countries taking part in the euro, has caused disagreements between Bonn and other European governments, notably France.
"The pact is a useful and very important initiative," Lamfalussy said in Le Monde.
The Germans proposed the pact because they are worried that lax budget policies after the launch of the euro will undermine its strength and expose the German economy to inflation.
They have sought to define numerically circumstances under which countries will be fined for running excessive deficits and also temporary situations which would exempt them from fines.
France and others do not want numerical definitions of the temporary circumstances and France wants the EU's council of finance ministers to have the power to decide.

"It will have a dissuasive effect," Lamfalussy said of the pact. "But, even if this pact is respected, we can conceive of sudden changes in the financing needs of a large country with unnacceptable consequences for others."

"To avoid this, there must be ex ante coordination of policies. Finance ministers must agree among themselves, talk among themselves. It would be important for this to imagine an appropriate mechanism."
Lamfalussy said that while outside control of the European Central Bank's policy would be in complete contradiction to the Maastricht Treaty, a dialogue about that policy would not.
"It would be in the interests of the ECB as well as the governments," he said of this dialogue.
Lamfalussy also said the U.S. dollar remained too cheap, saying: "At its current level compared to the principal European currencies, the dollar seems to me still undervalued," he told the newspaper.
The United States could get away with a weak dollar because of the currency's role as a reserve currency, he said.

"If we want to make the euro a true alternative in international financial marketplaces, the euro must have credibility and stability. This depends on the policies followed for the euro," Lamfalussy said.
"To the extent that the European Central Bank can effectively follow a policy of price stability and create a zone of internal stability, the currency will acquire very great strength."
